TESTIMONY OF ALICIA REA, ESQ. LD 1076 - Ought Not to Pass
An Act to Hire School Security Officers to Protect Students and Make Schools Safer
Joint Standing Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs April 23, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, greetings. My name is Alicia Rea, and I am a policy fellow at the ACLU of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions. On behalf of our members, I urge you to oppose LD 1076.
In 2019, the University of Southern Maine's Catherine Cutler Institute released Maine's first ever statewide study of school-based policing.1 The Cutler Institute's report confirms that school resource officer and school security officer programs simply do not work.2 Other studies have shown that SRO presence in schools does not make students feel safer.3 Students of color feel especially vulnerable in the presence of school officers.4 This is unsurprising, given that school officers disproportionately discipline students of color and students with disabilities.5 When in schools, law enforcement officers do what they are trained to do--detain, handcuff, and arrest. This leads to greater student alienation and a more threatening school climate.
Moreover, school security officers compete for scarce school funds with counselors and social workers. For example, prior to ending the SRO

program, the Portland School District spent over $150,000 per year on its two SROs.6 In recuperating that sum, Portland Public Schools was able to invest in de-escalation training.7 Schools should not be a place that funnels youth toward the criminal justice system. Schools should be places of enlightenment and growth, where students feel safe and supported. They should be a place where students are free from physical and psychological harm. This bill would move Maine away from this ideal, toward a more robust school-to-prison pipeline. Safe and healthy schools lead with support, not police. Please vote that LD 1076 ought not to pass.

AN ACT TO HIRE SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICERS TO PROTECT STUDENTS AND MAKE SCHOOLS SAFER
April 23, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Eileen King, the Executive Director of the Maine School Superintendents Association, testifying on behalf of the MSSA Legislative Committee neither for nor against L.D. 1076, An Act to Hire School Security Officers to Protect Students and Make Schools Safer.
The safety of students continues to be a top concern for both school boards and superintendents. In light of incidents of gun violence, both nationwide and within Maine, school leaders across the state are implementing new security features (such as reinforced entranceways and wearable "panic buttons" for staff), adding more security officers, and working even more closely with local law enforcement to ensure students and staff are safe.

PAST PRESIDENT PATRICIA HOPKINS
MSAD 11 GARDINER, 04345

While our association appreciates any efforts to improve the security in our school buildings, we do have questions about whether L.D. 1076 contains enough training or safeguards to ensure officers have the proper knowledge to handle violent incidents and best protect our students.

EILEEN E. KING EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
49 COMMUNITY DRIVE AUGUSTA ME 04330 (207) 622-3473 (800) 660-8484

We believe further clarity is needed about the duties of a "school security officer" in L.D. 1076, and whether this is solely for security at school functions, or if these officers would be in school hallways every day. Multiple districts have told us that they already hire "security monitors" - in some cases, former military officers or game wardens - who have previous experience in various law enforcement careers and are able to apply that experience towards protecting students. They then receive additional training in areas they are lacking. This model has been an incredibly successful avenue of leveraging the knowledge of our community members, and we would advocate for the legislature to look towards these kinds of models to improve school security, instead of creating a new school security officer position and training program.
Our group believes that the legislature should listen to the experiences of these school districts, as well as the knowledge of groups such as the Maine School Safety Center and the Maine Chiefs of Police Association - we believe together, they can help offer solutions to better protect our students.

Leading for equity, excellence and opportunity for all Maine Students

Statement in opposition to
L.D. 1076, An Act to Hire School Security Officers to Protect Students and Make Schools Safer
Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
April 23, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and honorable members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee. My name is Jason Moen. I am the Chief of the Auburn Police Department, and President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am submitting testimony on behalf of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association in opposition to LD 1076.
The mission of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association is to secure a closer official and personal relationship among Maine Police Officials; to secure a unity of action in law enforcement matters; to enhance the standards of police personnel, police training and police professionalism generally; to devise ways and means for equality of law enforcement throughout the state of Maine; to advance the prevention and detection of crime; to prescribe to the Law Enforcement Code of Ethics; and to promote the profession of law enforcement as an integral and dedicated force in today's society sworn to the protection of life and property.
All persons interested in a career in law enforcement must complete the Basic Law Enforcement Training Program (BLETP), an 18-week residential program at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy. The application process for the BLETP has two stages. The first stage consists of a personal history statement, a reading and writing examination, a physical fitness assessment, and a personal interview. Upon successfully completing this portion, an applicant continues with the second stage, which includes a fitness assessment, a background investigation, a psychological evaluation, and a polygraph examination.
Only full-time law enforcement officers who are employed in a law enforcement capacity or a person making an application to and being accepted as a tuition student can attend the BLETP. If a law enforcement agency hires you as a full-time law enforcement officer, you must complete the BLETP within one year.

During the BLETP, cadets focus on areas such as defensive tactics, use of force, verbal and nonverbal de-escalation techniques, appropriate strategies for interacting with people who have developmental disabilities, including autism, and recognizing the signs of someone experiencing a mental health crisis. This rigorous program is designed to thoroughly prepare law enforcement officers for all situations they may face protecting their communities.
Throughout Maine, school districts can provide added security within their buildings and property through school resource officers (SROs). SROs are law enforcement officers who work in public schools and who, by virtue of public employment, are vested with a duty to make arrests for crimes, whether that duty extends to all crimes or is limited to specific crimes.
LD 1076 creates a program that allows municipal police departments and county sheriff's offices to hire personnel specifically as school security officers. These officers, who are different from SROs, must be trained by the Maine Criminal Justice Academy and certified as part-time law enforcement officers under the preservice training program.
As this bill is drafted, it would establish a class of police officers who work full time but who would not be required to receive the extensive training as provided in the BLETP. Should this bill pass, school districts may pressure their local police departments or sheriff's offices to provide security officers through this route due to funding constraints.
Any emergency can occur on school property, whether it be a fight between students, a crisis intervention, or an active shooter situation. Any officer working to protect the school community needs to be prepared for the unexpected. That is precisely what the BLETP does. Law enforcement officers who have been entrusted with ensuring the safety of our community's most vulnerable members should not be trained to a lower standard than those patrolling the streets.
For these reasons, we oppose the passage of LD 1076 and ask the committee to vote ought not to pass.
10045821:
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Opposition to
LD 1076 - An Act to Hire School Security Officers to Protect Students and Make Schools Safer
April 23, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am submitting testimony in opposition to LD 1076, at the direction of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). Our LPC is made up of individuals from across Maine with municipal officials elected by their peers across Maine's 35 Senate districts representing communities with very different access to available enforcement resources and local capacity.
The role of a police officer in a school setting extends far beyond physical security. These professionals are deeply connected to their school community and establish important schoolcommunity relationships. These officers usually are armed, and in uniform, making them distinguishable in an emergency by outside responders should that be necessary. They have received extensive training in topics related to school-based law enforcement like legal issues specific to schools and adolescent development. In addition to their specialized roles that require continuous training and evaluation, they must also be connected to an agency that can investigate outside the school setting to ensure proper investigation of disclosed incidents occurring away from the school, protecting victims, and any chain of evidence.
A successful school resource officer is far more mentor than an enforcer and strives to create a bank of positive police interactions with the school community that carry on into the community at-large. Because of this, municipal officials believe a "security only" approach, which this bill implies misses the point on why communities add these individuals to their school rosters. Without a relationship with a law enforcement agency, and continued training on adolescent interaction, mentoring and policing, these individuals would just be security guards in a school setting which has been shown to be detrimental to the law enforcement-adolescent relationship.
Additionally, well-trained retired individuals would be welcomed to join any police department and apply for these roles currently. This would provide them with the continued training necessary to be successful in their role and additional experienced staffing for local agencies who struggle with recruitment. For these reasons, municipal officials ask that oppose

LD 1076 and ask that the committee consider keeping municipal, and county school resource officers connected to their communities and agencies, rather than move to a security officer model that could undermine these important community relationships.

MAINE COUNCIL OF SCHOOL BOARD ATTORNEYS
Isabel Ekman, Esq., Chair

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 1076
AN ACT TO HIRE SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICERS TO PROTECT STUDENTS AND MAKE SCHOOLS SAFER
April 23, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Steven Bailey, the Executive Director of the Maine School Boards Association, testifying on behalf of the MSBA Legislative Committee in opposition to L.D. 1076, An Act to Hire School Security Officers to Protect Students and Make Schools Safer.
We appreciate any efforts to better protect students and staff, but our association is concerned that this bill, as written, could have unintended consequences that could result in officers not receiving the necessary training to best protect our children.
Our first question with this bill is how this new class of "school security officers" would differ from school resource officers, who are already in schools across Maine. The bill appears to describe these officers as contracted positions that would "provide school security-related functions and services." How would these duties differ from those of current trained officers? Could school security officers arrest people? Could they be in school, full-time, working with students? Or would they primarily be used for extra security at an event or sports game? School leaders see value in having the option to hire additional officers for certain security-related functions, but we believe more clarity is needed in the language of the bill.
In discussing this bill with law enforcement, we also have concerns that the training requirements may not meet a strict enough standard to ensure these officers are equipped to succeed in protecting students and staff. Our schools and police departments are proud that School Resource Officers are the best of our community's law enforcement personnel, well-versed in student safety, emergency preparedness, and youth mental health needs. To be qualified for these roles requires months of training in the classroom and in the field. We are concerned that the unclear language for training for school security officers in L.D. 1076 may not meet these high standards.
We would defer to other groups, such as the Maine School Safety Center and the Maine Chiefs of Police Association, who better understand the on-the-ground knowledge and skills required for each of these law enforcement positions and could better speak to how those requirements interact with the language proposed in L.D. 1076.
Again, our association appreciates any efforts to increase school safety and security, but we believe the language and potential unintended consequences must be better understood before this bill moves forward.
